lyrics.title: Lyrics
lyrics.noneHelp: Add them to the file's tags, or put an .lrc file with the same name next to it.
lyrics.noneOnline: Neither the file nor LRCLIB has them. An .lrc file with the same name next to the track works too.
lyrics.onlineHelp: Asks LRCLIB, a free lyrics database, by the track's title, artist, album and length. You can turn this off in Settings.
lyrics.settingHelp: When a track has no lyrics of its own, ask LRCLIB (lrclib.net) for them. It gets the track's title, artist, album and length.

err.noAudio: There are no audio files in what you dropped. Supported: FLAC, WAV, AIFF, ALAC, MP3, OGG.

error.deviceNotFound: device not found — was it unplugged?

error.rateRefused: the device doesn't accept {rate} kHz in exclusive mode
error.rateStuck: the device didn't switch to {rate} kHz (still at {current} kHz)

test.title: Channel check
test.subtitle: First a low tone in the left ear, then a high one in the right
display.label: Display
step.downmix: {from} mixed down to {to}, {db} dB so it never clips
step.headroomPending: {db} dB of headroom against clipping (while the track loads)
verdict.empty: Add music to the queue and the signal path to your headphones will appear here.
verdict.test: First a low tone in the left ear, then a high one in the right. If it's the other way round, the channels are swapped.
verdict.dop: The DAC gets the file's DSD stream bit for bit, packed as DoP.
verdict.iosVolume: The DAC gets the file's samples, but the iPhone volume is below maximum, so iOS may recalculate them. For bit-perfect playback, set the iPhone volume to maximum and adjust the volume on the DAC.
verdict.bitPerfect: The DAC gets exactly the samples stored in the file.
verdict.network: The network player gets exactly the samples stored in the file.
verdict.lossy: The file is lossy-compressed. The DAC gets the decoded signal unchanged.
verdict.clip: The signal hits 0 dBFS: the equalizer raises the level too much.
dsd.exclusive: DoP works only in exclusive mode
dsd.volume: for DoP the iPhone volume must be at maximum; adjust the volume on the DAC
dsd.dsp: the equalizer and crossfeed work on PCM
dsd.rate: {device} doesn't run at {rate} kHz, which DoP {dsd} needs
dsd.channels: the file has more channels ({n}) than the device, and DoP can't mix them down
enh.upsamplingHelp: Resamples the track to the highest rate of the same family that the DAC accepts ({a} → {b}, 48 → 384). Linear-phase filter, about 100 dB of stopband attenuation.
enh.eqHelp: Parametric and graphic EQ with presets per output, linear phase, convolution and import from AutoEQ, Equalizer APO, Wavelet and REW.
enh.crossfeedHelp: Mixes a softer copy of the opposite channel into each ear, as when you listen to speakers. Removes the “sound inside your head” feeling on recordings with hard-panned stereo.
enh.headroomHelp: After decoding, MP3 peaks often go past 0 dBFS, and loud passages crackle. The player measures the overshoot across the whole track and lowers the level by exactly that much, usually less than 1 dB.
enh.restoreHelp: Finds where the codec cut off the highs (16–19 kHz for 128–256 kbps MP3) and rebuilds the octave above from the harmonics of the band below. It's a plausible reconstruction, not a return of what was lost. Files cut off above 20 kHz are left alone.
enh.losslessNote: Lossless files aren't affected by these settings; they play as before.
enh.footerLossy: Lossless files go to the DAC bit-perfect, MP3 and AAC with corrections.
enh.footerPure: Everything is off: the signal goes to the DAC bit-perfect.
enh.footerOn: Enhancers turn bit-perfect off. Turn them all off to get the untouched signal back.
dev.networkSearching: Looking for Sonos, WiiM, Bluesound, Chromecast and other UPnP/DLNA and Google Cast players on this network…
dev.networkHelp: The music goes to the player over your network as FLAC, sample for sample. For bit-perfect sound, keep the player's own EQ and volume leveling off.
dev.iosNote: iPhone plays through one output: whichever is connected now. Connect a DAC over USB-C and the sound goes to it at the file's sample rate. Other apps go quiet meanwhile.
dev.androidExclusiveHelp: Android 14 and later hand the USB DAC over to the player entirely: no Android mixer, no system volume, and the DAC's rate follows each track. Adjust the volume on the DAC.
dev.exclusiveHelp: Other apps can't mix in their sound, and the DAC's rate follows each track.
dev.dopHelp: DSD files go to {device} as they are, up to DSD{max}. Turn this on only if the DAC supports DoP: otherwise you'll hear quiet noise instead of music. When it's off, DSD is converted to PCM.
dev.testHelp: First a low tone on the left, then a high one on the right.
dev.speaker: Speaker
lib.label: Library

lib.androidHelp: The library is the Music folder in the phone's internal storage. Copy albums there over USB from a computer or with any file manager. Android doesn't show apps DSD files (DSF, DFF) in Music, so put those in Android/data/dev.local.hifi/files/Music.
lib.iosHelp: The library is the app's folder: Files → On My iPhone → BitSpring. Copy albums there with the Files app or with Finder on a Mac (iPhone → Files), or add files here.

lib.emptyAndroid: Copy albums to the Music folder in the phone's internal storage, over USB from a computer or with a file manager, then tap “Rescan”. If the app asked for access to music, allow it.
lib.emptyIos: Copy albums to Files → On My iPhone → BitSpring (or from a Mac with Finder: iPhone → Files → BitSpring) and the library will find them by itself. Or add files from here.
lib.emptyDesktop: Choose a folder with music, such as Music in your home folder or an external drive. The files stay where they are: the app only reads tags and artwork.

eq.title: Equalizer
eq.importHelp: Reads Equalizer APO and Peace, AutoEQ (ParametricEQ, GraphicEQ, CSV), Wavelet, REW, EasyEffects and foobar2000 presets.
eq.hpPopular: Popular headphones. Type a model to search the whole AutoEQ catalog.
eq.hpFirst: First {n} of {total}: type more to narrow it down
eq.hpWhich: Measured by several people. The first is usually the most accurate.
eq.hpNoneOffline: Only popular models are here until the full catalog loads.
eq.hpOffline: The full catalog didn't download, so only popular models are listed.
eq.hpCredit: Profiles by AutoEQ (Jaakko Pasanen, MIT licence), from measurements by oratory1990, crinacle, Rtings and others.
eq.pasteHint: Paste the text of an Equalizer APO or AutoEQ preset, for example as copied from autoeq.app.
eq.emptyTitle: Shape the sound to your headphones
eq.emptyText: Start from a template, or bring in a correction someone has measured for your model: AutoEQ, Equalizer APO, Wavelet and REW files all work.
eq.name: Preset name
eq.compareHelp: Plays without the equalizer at the same average loudness, so you judge the tone, not the volume.
eq.comparing: Without the equalizer, at the same loudness. Press Compare again to hear it.
eq.phaseHelp.minimum: Minimum phase, like an analog equalizer: no pre-ringing, and every change is heard at once.
eq.phaseHelp.linear: Linear phase: no phase shift at any frequency. Sharp, deep cuts can pre-ring before transients. Changes are heard after about half a second.
eq.autoHelp: Lowers the level by exactly the highest boost, so the equalizer can never clip.
eq.clipWarn: With this preamp the curve goes above 0 dBFS and loud passages will clip. Turn on Auto or lower the preamp.
eq.noBands: No bands yet. Double-click the graph where you want one, or add one below.
eq.irHelp: A WAV, FLAC or AIFF impulse response, mono or stereo, up to 6 seconds: room correction made in REW, rePhase or Dirac, or a headphone response. It's applied after the equalizer, and its main peak is lined up so the music stays in time.
eq.editorHelp: Drag a point to change its frequency and gain; scroll over it to change Q. Double-click the graph to add a band. With a point focused, the arrow keys move it (Shift for bigger steps), [ and ] change Q, Delete removes it.
upd.title: Updates
upd.restartNote: The app restarts to finish, which stops playback.
upd.androidNote: Android will ask you to confirm the installation.
error.installNotAllowed: allow BitSpring to install apps on the settings screen that just opened, then press Download and install again
tags.note: Tags are written into the files themselves; the audio in them stays exactly as it is.
tags.readOnly: DSD files and tracks of a CUE image can't be edited here.
q.d.genuineFull: The music fills the file's whole frequency range. No sign of conversion.
q.d.genuineHigh: The music reaches {khz} kHz, beyond what a CD can hold.
q.d.genuineFade: The highs fade out gradually from about {khz} kHz, as in many recordings. No sign of conversion.
q.d.upsampled: Nothing above {khz} kHz: this {rate} kHz file was made from a CD-quality one (44.1 or 48 kHz). It sounds the same as that file and only takes more space.
q.d.mirror: Above {khz} kHz there is only a mirror image of the music below it, the trace a simple resampler leaves. This {rate} kHz file was made from a {from} kHz one: it sounds the same and only takes more space.
q.d.fromLossy: Everything above {khz} kHz is cut off sharply, the way MP3 and AAC encoders do it. A lossless copy can't bring back what they removed.
q.d.padded: The lowest 8 bits of every sample are zero: this is 16-bit audio stored in a 24-bit file.
q.d.lossy: MP3, AAC and Vorbis leave out part of the sound by design, so there's nothing to unmask here.
q.d.dsd: DSD fills the top of its range with noise by design, so this check doesn't apply.
q.d.short: Too short or too quiet to judge.
q.d.wallAmbiguous: The music stops sharply at {khz} kHz. MP3 at its best settings does that, and so do many CD masters.
q.d.gradualLow: Little above {khz} kHz, and the highs fade out gradually instead of stopping. It may be an old recording, or a file made from a CD or 48 kHz master with a gentle filter.
q.note: Checked on this device, from the sound itself. A verdict is a strong hint, not proof.
